segs: REFLECTING ON CONVERSATIONS
KINGDOM OF COUCHES • CHAPTER EXCERPT
Community is not simply another ministry activity; it is the context
for all ministry activities. It is the environment in which spiritual
growth takes place. And since community is central to our model for
spiritual growth, a few planned socials are not going to get the job
done. We needed a resource to elevate community, encourage it, and
teach it.
Will Walker’s book is probably the best apologetic written for why
community is the matrix for spiritual growth. But the content goes
well beyond theological reasoning, providing extremely practical
how’s and why’s for living out our faith in community. Through
excellent writing and reasoning, personal examples and stories, the
book creates a hunger and desire for communal living.
Content of Book: Why We Pursue Independence; Why We Need
Community; Repentance; Community and the Word-Communal
Quiet Times, Community and Confession; Group Prayer; Godly
Speech and Conversation, and A Commitment to Live Communally.

D R I N K I N G
G A M E S
Sometimes I wake up with what feels like a hangover. As best as
I can remember, an actual hangover feels like bankruptcy—spent,
impoverished, regretful. That is how I feel some mornings, only
without the obvious explanation for why. I still have to get up on
these days, if not for work then because my four-year-old is jump-
ing on the bed. So I’ll drag myself across the floor to the bathroom.
My friend Rick says that you are never more yourself than when
you are on the toilet. “It is the place of ultimate humility,” he
says. “Can you think of a place where you would least want to be
seen than on the toilet?” I tell you this because the last time I felt
bankrupt, God spoke to me precisely in that place, the place of
humility. He kept bringing a verse to my mind: “Everyone who
drinks this water will be thirsty again, but whoever drinks the
water I give him will never thirst.”1
Jesus told that to a woman one day when she had gone to
draw water from a well. He was saying that the water from the
well would only last for a little while. Eventually she would have
to come back and draw more. He was using water, something
she depended upon for survival, to reveal Himself as the Living
Water––what she needed for life.
1 John 4:13, NIV
© 2010, CruPress, All Rights Reserved. CruPress.com
I have plenty of water, that’s not the problem. I can turn on
the faucet and watch it trickle out for hours. I don’t because that
would be irresponsible, but I could. No, the thirsts in my life are
for things like acceptance and fun and deeper meaning. The wells
I go to are as real as the thirsts––working or watching television
or talking, for example. Talking. Conversation is such an easy
place for me to go to find what I’m looking for. I use my words as
bait for things like approval and value––temporary redemption. I
say things, often not because I mean them, but because I want to
sound cool or smart or funny. I want to convince people that I’m
the kind of person that means the things I say.
This usually works. For a time. The reality is, though, that when
you try to get what you need from the wrong places, you just feel
empty again. When you keep drinking from these wells, you only
find temporary satisfaction. Conversation is important. It’s central
to our lives. But it’s often draining and empty. I talk so much about
things that don’t matter, about how traffic’s bad during rush hour
or about how it’s taking a long time for our waiter to bring us our
food. People know these things; they don’t need to be made aware.
Even worse, sometimes my words are directly hurtful. I like
to blame most of these instances on other people’s ignorance or
inability.
I feel bad about sticking my foot in my mouth; I never intend
to. I wonder though, if I would slip up so frequently if I approached
conversations out of an interest and love for people instead of a
desire to get people to like me? That sounds simplistically noble,
and it is. But our words quickly come to reflect what we’re really
hoping for, regardless of how hard we try to mask it. I need water,
but I’m in even greater need of Living Water. When we get what
we need from the right source, instead of from a temporary well,
we can rest because we are internally satisfied. Jesus says that this
internal kind of satisfaction is like a natural spring—fresh water,
always flowing. We would always have something to give because
of this. Giving would come naturally because we would not need
© 2010, CruPress, All Rights Reserved. CruPress.com
to take from anyone, not need to be redeemed by what others can
give.
The reason you feel so terrible when you wake up after drinking
too much is because your body is dehydrated. The dryness inside
gives you an awful headache. What you drank has actually taken
out more than it has put in. Conversations are full of these shallow
wells, promising life but actually making life more miserable. The
more shallowly I drink the more I dry up, dehydrated, hung over.
Silence is no more an answer than refusing water, our words just
need to be valued for what they are worth––which is sometimes
more and other times less than we think.
I have spent a lot of time in conversation with Brett over the
past year or so. While I am always talking, he is always observing:
Why do people say the things they say? Why are people saying so
many words and yet communicating so little? How do I lovingly
get Will to stop talking for a few minutes? I guess you could say
that Brett has walked me through more than a few hangovers.
After wrestling with this chapter—and losing—it finally occurred
to me that Brett has probably thought more about the dynamics
of conversation than anyone I know. So I asked him to write this
chapter. He probably wanted to write it all along but couldn’t
get me to stop talking long enough to tell me. That’s okay. I like
when things are my idea anyway. Without further babble from me,
welcome to the thoughts of Brett Westervelt.
C O L O R I N G
B O O K S
This is a chapter about conversation. About why we say the
things we say. In all honesty, I don’t know exactly what motivates
the words we speak or withhold, and my own motivations are
often murky. The words we read and hear each day come from a
thousand different angles for a thousand different reasons. It’s the
same with our conversations, where language has its back and
forth; where it’s often what goes unsaid that speaks the most. I
© 2010, CruPress, All Rights Reserved. CruPress.com
won’t pretend to have the guidelines for each and every one of the
verbal interactions that ground our lives; that would be foolish of
me, and would take a long time. Instead I’ll offer some looks into
my thoughts on the matter and bring in some second opinions––
different angles on the same thing––hoping that we find some-
thing insightful here. These thoughts may not line up perfectly;
they might overlap or exist completely independent of each other.
But getting a group of people together to discuss something usually
leads to that. There’s a certain beauty in the disconnectedness.
Conversation is frustrating to me. I tend to be pretty optimistic
about life in general, sometimes wondering why the glass has to be
only half full. I also tend to (over)analyze life, constantly develop-
ing theories and philosophies that I’m sure must be right because
they make perfect sense to me. Optimism and theorizing can be
problematic as they’re quick avenues away from reality. Conversa-
tion is frustrating to me precisely because it’s so utterly grounded
in what is in fact the case.
It’s quite easy for me to start thinking that a girl likes me. I can
think those thoughts and interpret situations that make her unde-
clared love for me the only realistic possibility. Maybe I ran into
her at a coffee shop where she smiled at me in a way not unlike
the way Meg Ryan smiled at Tom Hanks in that movie You’ve Got
Seattle. It’s fate. It’s the ongoing conversation we have in which
she finds ways to casually mention her boyfriend that clue me in to
the reality of the situation.
I always picture my friends and I, having these amazing discus-
sions that sometimes lead to punches being thrown and other
times lead to tears. I like to think we’re all pretty passionate. I’ll
watch a movie like The Royal Tenenbaums or The Breakfast Club
and think it likely that I will soon find myself exchanging witty
dialogue with lots of hidden meaning that eavesdroppers will
carefully analyze. This rarely happens. It turns out none of us have
anyone to write our lines.
I hear people talk about the lost art of conversation, how con-
© 2010, CruPress, All Rights Reserved. CruPress.com
versation used to be an art form and how it’s much more like col-
oring within clearly marked lines now. Like in a coloring book. I
imagine this to be true, though I have no such past art to compare
my current conversations with. One thought is that we don’t know
how to talk to other people because we watch television too much
and our brains have atrophied. I wonder, though, if the real reason
our conversations are often so draining and empty is because we’re
afraid of each other.
We are afraid of what people might think if they knew what we
actually thought. We fear looking stupid. I’m fine if the conversa-
tion stays on impersonal topics like sports or the weather or how
that guy’s outfit does little to compliment his body type. I tend to
speak my mind about those kinds of things, because there’s not a
whole lot hinging on my opinion. Wait, you think it’s unseasonably
warm this fall? That’s ridiculous. Our friendship is over.
It’s when things get personal that I begin to keep my actual
thoughts private. Ask me what I think about gay marriage or
if Hindus go to hell or how I feel about the outfit that you are
wearing, and I quickly become guarded. I’m much more likely to
spout out the right answer or the easy answer instead of my actual
thoughts, coloring well within the lines of social protocol. It’s not
that I really want to be dishonest. The pretense is draining; it’s
dehydrating. It’s just that honesty is risky; it’s rarely politically cor-
rect. It’s easier to lie or to just keep things impersonal.
What I sacrifice along the way is meaningful relationship,
keeping people at arms length for fear of losing them. I could term
all lighthearted conversation “shallow,” labeling small talk as the
enemy here, but it’s not. I’m willing to debate at great lengths the
tracks essential to a Ryan Adams “Best of,” and frankly, Vince
Young’s Heisman chances are an important topic of conversation.
If I were female, I might even find it in my heart to spend a few
hours discussing the latest issue of InStyle. Talk of this sort is a
lot of fun, and it’s the normal person’s way to transition to more
serious matters. It would be strange for me to go up to a complete
© 2010, CruPress, All Rights Reserved. CruPress.com
stranger and ask them about the greatest tragedy or triumph
they’ve ever experienced.
It’s my attempts at acceptance––to please or appease those
around me––that send my conversations awry. I find myself
launching into diatribes about things I care little about, like how
things written in italics should really be spoken differently. I camp
out on the lighthearted and meaningless, even as I am really won-
dering about entirely different things. I use my words to manipu-
late, twist, or avoid difficult realities.
A few months ago I was on the phone with my sister, and after
we had talked for a while, she could tell there was something
wrong with me. I claimed to be tired, and she let it go. Really,
I was feeling pretty depressed at the time, and after we said our
goodbyes, I went and wrote about that very thing in my jour-
nal. It’s not difficult to be honest and bold in a journal. But in
conversation, with all of the instant feedback, with fears of being
misunderstood, with the risk of being let down, it’s easier to lie.
It’s easier to disconnect my thoughts from my words, to color
within the lines of expectations. It’s this thinking and speaking
disconnect that makes conversation grueling, that drives me to my
journal and away from lasting friendship.
There are solutions to this conundrum. Like drinking alco-
hol. My friend Doug was at a wedding a few months ago when a
friend, with the aid of a few glasses of wine, told him that in her
opinion, procreation was the only real point to life. Doug, initially
startled by the bluntness of this statement, went on to have a
good, substantial conversation with this person, someone who had
previously been closed off to in any way discussing her beliefs. Our
friend Jeremy calls alcohol “liquid courage,” because after you’ve
had a few glasses, you find yourself saying what you would have
been much too composed to otherwise mention. Being inebriated
makes it hard to have both an internal and external monologue,
so they usually just turn into the same thing. Meaningful con-
versation often results, based on real people’s actual thoughts;
© 2010, CruPress, All Rights Reserved. CruPress.com
it’s just a shame that really knowing someone requires temporary
brain damage and a headache in the morning. (One might dare to
propose that there is even a divine design behind drinking wine in
moderation. But due to the fear of others, exposing myself, risking
rejection, causing friction, and being politically incorrect: I’ll keep
that thought to myself. Well, at least hidden in parentheses.)
Nevertheless, the blog has been a healthier way for me to open
up. The thoughts I was writing in my journal became thoughts
that I was sharing with others. The writing process has allowed me
to let go of these thoughts slowly instead of all at once. I can read
what I’ve written to make sure it speaks to what I’m trying to say
before passing it on to Will or Bob or David––a trusted few that
I’ve gotten past trying to impress. Finally, I’ll post my thoughts on
the blog for anyone to read and comment on. I’ve found myself
writing things I never thought I would even admit to pondering,
and as a result I’ve found myself in engaging, thought-provoking
conversation. It’s not what I would have expected. Along the way
I’ve developed some deep friendships––I’ve found people worth
crying with or punching. People that I genuinely know and love.
I M A G E
M A N A G E M E N T
Will and I spend the bulk of our days with an extraordinary
group of students at the University of Texas. One of the girls I am
getting to know is Tina. Tina is refreshing to be around because
she’s honest but not proud. Hilarious but also serious. One day
we got to talking about how important conversations are to the
health of a community.
Lately, all Tina really wants is to be known, good and bad, and
still be liked. She told me that and said that she has been telling
a lot of her friends the same thing, hoping they would take the
bait. “Nobody’s taking it,” she said. “It’s a good thing I guess—I
mean I am relieved for them in a way––because it’s asking a lot.”
The irony is that so many people feel the same way and want the
© 2010, CruPress, All Rights Reserved. CruPress.com
kind of honest and meaningful conversation that makes them feel
known, but do not act on it. Everyone is pretending not to want
what everyone wants.
Tina thinks we pretend because we are trying to avoid loneli-
ness. “We start developing personality traits that people attribute
to us. If you are known for your sarcasm you play it up. If people
think of you as the ‘cheery one’, you don’t let people know that
you have bad days. By focusing on a few personality traits, we
attempt to create an image we think others will like. If this image
is accepted, we can avoid loneliness, at least on the surface.” So I
asked her how she pretends. I love what she wrote in response:
I hide behind sarcasm. Many people like to say they
are sarcastic by nature. I used to feel the same way until
last week when I hurt a good friend with some misplaced
sarcasm. To make matters worse, I realized I had never
let this friend know how much he means to me until
after I had put my foot in my mouth. I’m cautious about
letting people know just how much they mean to me.
I’m afraid of giving of myself and finding out the feeling
isn’t mutual. I know that there are several people in my
life that I love that probably have no idea, but there
are plenty of people I love that have been the subject
of a “well-placed” sarcastic comment. I’m finding that
I use sarcasm as some kind of leverage I can hold over
other people because I am good at it, and not everyone
is. This pretending thing gets out of hand, though, and
we not only hurt ourselves but others, because we end
up dealing with each other superficially, never giving
each other the chance to be known.
Conversation is a world of ironies: I use conversations to make
people like or admire me, but the person that people come to like
and admire is a phantom, a persona that I’ve carefully constructed
© 2010, CruPress, All Rights Reserved. CruPress.com
to hide behind. It’s the difference between Simon and Garfunkel’s
Bridge Over Troubled Water and Kelly Clarkson’s Since You’ve Been
Gone. Everyone likes Since You’ve Been Gone––it’s shiny and pro-
duced and easy to sing-along to, but there’s little honesty there, no
depth of reality. Bridge Over Troubled Water may not be as catchy
on first listen, but it will move your soul, often in different ways
at different times. Chances are that in a few years you will have
forgotten about Since You’ve Been Gone, as great of pop as it may
be. It’s just that pop changes, while depth and honesty endure.
Phantom people suck the life out of community because they suck
out all of the reality and replace it with an easygoing facade. These
kinds of friendships are easier on the front end, but they rarely
endure.
We all need what we must give. Our stories are meant to be
shared; they’re realities that provide both discouragement and
encouragement––a way to tell of the past and whether it’s worth
repeating. A real self, with a unique personality and a perspective
gives life in a way that a caricature never could. And while it’s
true that we’re all imperfect, makeup is only a temporary fix, an
avoidance of reality. We will only experience conversations to be
life giving if our aim is to give life to others. God has set it up this
way. Whoever wants to keep life will lose it, and whoever gives life
will find it.
F R E E
F R O M
F E A R
Talking with people quickly reveals both our need for others
and our deep-seated need for what only God can provide. If we
could eavesdrop on our own conversations, we would realize how
much of what we say is to get attention or acceptance––to derive
popularity and redemption from our friends. And while people are
the wrong source for it, redemption is a most proper want, but it
will only come from God.
We need people to both know us and love us, but the grace
© 2010, CruPress, All Rights Reserved. CruPress.com
they need to deal with our faults will also only come from God.
They will be able to forgive, but only because, in Christ, God has
forgiven them much. The gospel provides a fertile ground for com-
munity, and for the kinds of conversations that community tends
to be grounded in. It’s tragic that this is often the opposite of our
experience.
Christian community can be the place where we pretend most.
David works at a church as a small groups pastor. Small groups are
designed for conversation, but if you have ever been in a small
group you know how meaningful conversations can be hard to
come by. Usually they end up being a contest to see who knows
the most stuff. David says the problem is not that we don’t say
meaningful things, but we know a bunch of stuff we may not actu-
ally believe. He elaborated on the blog:
Last week in a small group discussion a newcomer
spoke up saying, “I didn’t know we were going to be
this blunt. There are a few other things I probably need
to share.” I can’t remember the last time I was part of
a small group in which a visitor was struck by the level
of honesty and authenticity. All the small group Bible
studies, all the Sunday school classes, and all the church
services, and none of them have impressed most people
with their authenticity. Those gatherings could vari-
ously be described as educational, informative, chal-
lenging, fun, boring, unfriendly, and convicting—but
not blunt. Maybe blunt in teaching, but never in shar-
ing about what’s going on in our lives. Why?
Rather than beat up on the groups for not being more
authentic (especially since I’ve led many of them), I
want to pursue a different question: Why have I not
shared bluntly in those groups when given the oppor-
tunity? Why did I ask for prayer for more discipline
when the reality was compulsive habits controlled my
© 2010, CruPress, All Rights Reserved. CruPress.com
life and a little more discipline was unlikely to make a
difference?
Here’s one example of many that relate to this situ-
ation. I’m not sure that I believe Paul when he says
there is no condemnation in Christ.2 I know that is
true somewhere in the record book of heaven, but I
am not so sure about here on Earth, especially in my
Bible study. Share about sin or struggle in your life that
you have no solution for in that context, and you will
wish you had merely passed gas. The response is about
the same—awkward shifting and glancing around, a
few mumbled comments, a lame attempt at humor to
relieve the tension, maybe some advice to avoid this
happening again.
But if there really is no condemnation, why should I
let other people keep me from being honest? I care too
much about what others think about me, and in doing
so, I continue to construct a pitifully weak foundation
to prop myself upon rather than depending, with all
my weight, on God’s truth. I pass on the opportunity
to invite others into deeper relationship. Jesus spoke
about two men who built on different foundations.
They both heard His words, but only one took action
as if those words were true. Somehow I want the firm
foundation without the counterculture risk involved in
actually living my life there.
2 Romans 8:1, NIV

I WA S N ’ T
P R E PA R E D
This summer I spent a few weeks overseas. There were twelve
of us, and we spent our time studying the language and culture of
our host country, making friends with students at the university
we were at, and praying for and getting opportunities to share the
gospel with them.
Culture is a strange thing. You don’t realize how much of your
life is only the way it is because of where you live until you live
somewhere else for a while. It turns out the rest of the world
doesn’t think that English is as important as I’ve come to think.
Most of the people where I lived got along just fine speaking a dif-
ferent language entirely. I generally take conversation for granted.
This was not the case overseas, because communication that I
could actually understand and take part in was infinitely less avail-
able. This is what I wrote in my journal a few days after our arrival:
I sometimes feel as though words have lost their sig-
nificance. In a world of information, there are so many
words that each word carries little weight. We either
say much, with little consequence—in effect adding to
the noise or we say nothing at all—choosing to see our
lives as boring or our experiences as not worth retell-
ing. Both extremes treat words and stories as worthless,
not as beautiful and powerful.
It’s entirely different being in a place where I can’t
understand the language. The noise around me of idle
chatter is not much different than a car horn or a school
bell. I find myself starved for communication, whether
that be in the Word of God or with friends or on the
only English channel on my TV. Words, worthless in
their endless supply, have suddenly become valuable
again.
© 2010, CruPress, All Rights Reserved. CruPress.com
My frustration with language brought me to a place of deep
dependence on my teammates. I spent most of my days in interest-
ing but hackneyed conversation with the locals, attempting talk of
basketball or the gospel across a sometimes steep language barrier.
It was great and meaningful, but also draining. I would return to
my dormitory at night, hungry for pure, unadulterated English.
Back at the dorm my teammates and I would spend the rest of
the evening crammed in someone’s room, discussing the day and
life at hand to a depth that we’d been wanting to go for hours.
When we’d all met up in Ft. Worth a few weeks before, there was
plenty of silence. We were mostly introverts. In that dorm room
though, at the end of a foreign day, we needed conversation, and
we got to know each other like we’d known few others before. At
the same time we valued our words and tried to avoid using them
carelessly. You take amazing care with words when you only get to
speak a few.
We spent the brunt of these few hours each night asking ques-
tions of each other: What’s your family like? What’s been the
hardest thing about being here this summer? What are your top
five movies of all time? How did you come to faith in Christ? We
would take turns asking questions, often following the answers
with “Why?” and always delving deeper. I initially just wanted
someone to say something that I could understand, but I quickly
found interest in what my teammates were saying, and I wanted
to hear more. It’s amazing what you find out about people when
you ask them about themselves. In these conversations each of us
needed what the others had to give.
Being in a group of Christian English speakers in a primarily
non-Christian, non-English speaking country was essential to me.
I would have had a difficult, if not impossible, few weeks if not for
these others. Back in the States the reality is not as different as my
more independent life would reflect. My community is crucial, not
optional as I often treat it. I have a great need for the words that
only my Christian friends who know me deeply can speak. We
© 2010, CruPress, All Rights Reserved. CruPress.com
share experiences and a common language that is unique. Usually,
I alternate between noise and silence—forgetting the value of my
words to encourage and to challenge my friends, to make them
laugh (when appropriate), to console their tears, to keep them
aware that God is still near, to remind them that someone under-
stands. If we really have been sent here and are citizens of another
country, then a Christian community is foreign to this land.
Complete assimilation requires some precious losses, and often we
merge with society at large without ever realizing it.
T H E
P O W E R
O F
P O S I T I V E
S P E A K I N G
Will turned thirty this year, which is an age that is a factor of
ten, meriting more celebration than other birthdays. I myself was
surprised at his age, because on one hand Will has the wisdom of
someone much beyond thirty, and on the other hand he always
gets carded at concerts that are 21-and-up. I guess thirty is appro-
priate as an average between two extremes. Will wrote about this
milestone on the blog, and it has to do with what we’ve been talk-
ing about—conversation:
I turned thirty this year, which I did not think would
be that big of a deal to me. I was wrong. Someone told
me in college that your twenties are an adventure: that
you should try new things, meet new people, accumu-
late some experience, and be willing to fail. I have been
saying this since then, and also that you don’t need to
be good at anything until you are thirty. That is when
people start getting old, I thought, and by then you
should be able to identify some skills, preferably mar-
ketable skills. I am not going for humor here. This has
actually been the governing philosophy of my life for
the last decade. It is a good one, by the way, and if
you are twenty-something, you should believe this. It is
© 2010, CruPress, All Rights Reserved. CruPress.com
very comforting. You should also admit to yourself that
you are going to turn thirty in a very specific number
of days. This is where I went wrong, and now I am here
wondering how you go about figuring out what you are
good at. Perhaps I thought there would be some kind of
turning thirty Pentecost, where God would magically
impart skills. I had no such experience, though I did
cry twice this week.
Personally, I never think I am good at anything, but
now and then someone tells me that I am. If you look
at my life, you will see that I basically spend my time
and effort doing things that someone along the way
told me I was good at. Maybe I am a people pleaser,
but maybe it is also true that what we say to each other
in the way of encouragement and confidence is one of
the most powerful dynamics in the life of a community.
This week people close to me said some things that I
did not believe until they said them. Bob told me that
he loves me. Brett said he would follow me anywhere,
that he would probably do drugs if I did. [Editor’s note:
I meant this hypothetically.] Debbie said she believes
in me. I can’t tell you how rich these treasures are to
me.
I have been reading Philippians lately and cannot
help but notice how affectionate Paul is for the people
in Philippi. He calls them “dear friends” and “broth-
ers” and “partners in the gospel.” He would choose to
delay being in heaven to get the chance to visit them
again.3 I know that expressing affection for people can
be awkward, though I am unsure as to why. Whatever
the reason is though, we need to get over it. We need
to help people discover themselves, tell them why they
3 Philippians 1:25
© 2010, CruPress, All Rights Reserved. CruPress.com
are a blessing, talk about how God has gifted them and
how we see them being effective and fruitful in their
faith. We need to tell them that they belong. Everyone
is so desperate to belong.
Think about the disciples. Imagine what it would be
like to have Jesus (God) look you in the eye and say
that you belong to Him, that He believes in you, and
that He is going to use your influence to expand His
Kingdom throughout the world. In his Gospel, John
refers to himself as “the disciple that Jesus loves.”4 I
don’t think he was being arrogant. I think this was
simply the most central aspect of his identity, that Jesus
loved him.
The disciples turned the world upside down. What
would the people in your community do if they thought
about themselves as the one whom you love? This is
the irony of my twenty-something life philosophy: I
spent a decade trying to grow and develop so people
could tell me how great I am, but it turns out that life
is really more about telling others how great God is in
their life.
I’m only twenty three, so I have a few years to figure all of these
things out, but my limited experience leads me to firmly believe
what Will is saying. Encouragement is huge. That’s not overstat-

I’m not sure it’s possible to distill all we’ve been saying in this
chapter, but distillation has its purposes—“Love the Lord your
God with all your heart, soul, and mind and love your neighbor as
yourself”7 is a God-given distillation of the Law, a clear way to sum
it all up. My experience is that most of my empty conversations
stem from a self-focused attitude. I think my interactions with
people would look entirely different if I approached my words—
what and how much I said—with actual interest and concern for
others. It’s a heart-level change, really, and “out of the overflow
of the heart the mouth speaks.”8 Christ is at work restoring our
messed-up heart and the foul words that so often overflow, but we
would be amiss to think that we are uninvolved in the process.

When I go into a night of conversation with friends having
the self-centric attitude of a consumer, I usually leave frustrated
and empty. I spend a few hours gathering all I can in the way of
being listened to, laughed at, and verbally patted on the back. Get
a few people like me together and a competition quickly devel-
ops—all of us too busy talking and trying to impress to either learn
or listen. No one really hears each other because we are all too
busy thinking and talking about our own things.
Of course there are also those nights when it seems like no one
has anything to say. These kinds of conversation usually start off
with talk of the weather and head quickly and steadily towards
silence. Awkward silence. This is a different kind of consuming
conversation—I don’t feel like talking, and so I just wait for some-
one else to say something. I need conversation (I think that’s part
of not being lonely), but I’m going to wait around and let it come
to me. When an entire group of people starts thinking this way,
complaining or watching television quickly follows the silence.
Both are easy and inactive; both sacrifice community.
Good conversations involve both consuming and contributing:
giving and taking, and taking primarily to be able to give. I listen
and then I speak. I listen so that I can respond rightly, not so that
I can impress. I won’t ever find the redemption that I’m looking
for in the words or laughter of my friends, but I will find needed
encouragement. Strong conversation weaves people together,
and it only happens as we speak and listen, and as we are more
concerned with getting to know others than with proving what
we know. Knowledge puffs us up, often beyond recognition. Love
edifies.9

T A L K
T O
P E O P L E
Conversation is about relationship, and the most foundational
element of a relationship is not respect or common interests or
even love. It’s honesty. We can know each other only to the
degree that we are honest with each other. At the very point that
what I think and what I say I think differ, you can only relate to a
fake version of me, even if the fake me is just the real me, slightly
twisted—true relationship is suddenly not an option. In all of the
things we encounter in consumer-driven conversation—shallow
topics, saying stupid things, trying to impress, withdrawing—the
common ingredient is dishonesty. I realize this is a complex subject
and merely proposing honesty seems a bit elementary. I’m not
saying that honesty is the cure-all, but I am saying that it will go
a along way toward life-giving conversation. Honesty gets us into
more meaningful conversations where we feel known and there-
fore more interested in knowing others. Our honesty is a contribu-
tion that is uniquely our own. It sounds simple, but working it out
in actual life is anything but easy. As Bob wrote:
Honesty is an elusive concept. Most of the time
what I think is honesty is not honesty at all. My mind
is always forming judgments about people. Always. In
a room full of people, I’m forming mental categories:
that’s the flirty girl; there’s the geeky guy; over there
is the kid who talks too much. My judgments about
people are often a way of securing my place on the
social totem pole. Recognizing my own sinfulness in
this area, I usually conclude that honesty is not neces-
sarily the best policy. But now I am changing my mind
about that.
A major part of personal maturity is being able to
deal with our negative feelings in a godly way. Most
of the time what keeps me from being honest with
© 2010, CruPress, All Rights Reserved. CruPress.com
people is that I don’t want them to experience nega-
tive feelings. It’s easier not to tell the truth and keep
the peace than to tell the truth and create tension. By
not being honest I manipulate how others get to feel.
Protecting them from negative feelings deprives them
of the opportunity to deal with those feelings, which
keeps them from further sanctification. If people really
got their identity from Jesus—his crazy and unrealistic
grace and love—maybe I wouldn’t be so hesitant to be
honest with them. My honesty, no matter how hard
or sinful or ugly, could never undo the honesty of God
pouring His love into them at the core of their being.
I think that’s the kind of community Jesus intended
us to have; I’m just not sure we’re ready to believe the
gospel radically enough and do the hard work it takes
to create it.
The tension I feel in response to what Bob said is that it’s not
always appropriate or helpful to voice everything that we think,
and that in our honesty, we could be honestly wrong in our assess-
ments of others. Spewing our honest thoughts whenever we have
them is selfishness to the highest degree. I find it helpful to distin-
guish between selfish honesty and selfless honesty, honesty for the
purpose of consuming or for the purpose of contributing. Selfish
honesty is characterized by a sense of needing to say something
so you can feel better about yourself: gossip, insult, boasting, even
confession can be selfish when it’s just about getting it off your
chest. Selfless honesty, on the other hand, is characterized by a
sense of wanting to say something that benefits others: encourage-
ment, admonishment, teaching, personal disclosure for the sake of
intimacy, confession for the sake of restoration.
Our habits and inability to know all the factors in a given
situation make it difficult to discern our motives. That’s why it’s a
process of trial and error. That said, most of us tend to err on the
© 2010, CruPress, All Rights Reserved. CruPress.com
side of dishonesty. Pursuing or even thinking about the kind of
honesty that Bob describes is a push in the right direction.
In my estimation the most important aspect of honest conversa-
tion is facing the truth about our own lives, inviting others into
that process, and then humbly disclosing what we discover. We
talk as a means of being known as we truly are, not to impress, as
we want people to think we are. And as our words do turn to other
people, we need to think more about honesty in terms of encour-
aging one another and telling people the truth about how we see
God in them. This is woefully lacking in our communities. I sense
that if we told people the truth in the positive sense, telling them
the truth in the negative sense would not be as big of a deal.
Knowing what to say, how to say it, and when to say it requires
discernment, and discernment is not a formula but a process of
trial and error. Deciding to be honest is not a one-time purge
but a way of life that is navigated through the waters of success
and failure over time. Bob was right to say that gospel-centered
community is hard work. And perhaps the hardest work is that of
transforming our conversations. They have become such a stage
for self-importance, and we have so many habits from perform-
ing all these years. But we must start somewhere: we need to tell
people about the real us, and take interest in the real them as well.
T A L K I N G
P O I N T S
As a result of these discussions, our community has developed
some talking points. These are things for us to remember as we
approach conversation with each other. They are reminders of our
reality as believers and as individuals in a community. You might
find them helpful groundwork for your own conversations:
1. God is God: We do not need to solve everyone’s
problems, nor do we need everyone else to solve our
problems. We do not determine people’s worth, nor do
© 2010, CruPress, All Rights Reserved. CruPress.com
they determine ours. We do not know everything there
is to know. Not even close. We are not God, but God
is, and we approach what we say with this in mind.
2. You are you: You are not what you say. You can be
wrong or stupid and still be valuable, even right and
smart in other ways. Do not calculate everything you
are going to say to appear better than you are, as if your
worth depended on it. You simply don’t know what you
don’t know. There is grace to be found in the revealing
of our shortcomings.
3. Talking is talking: If you can’t say it, you probably
don’t know it. And you can’t know exactly what you
are going to say before you say it. Fearing people’s reac-
tions to what you are going to say hinders honest con-
versation. You need people’s feedback to your honest
thoughts. Only then can you trade your thoughts for
someone else’s. It’s like poker. You have to put your
cards on the table to get new ones.
4. Questions are informative: If you want to know
something about someone, ask them. If you want some-
one to do something, ask them. A direct question gives
someone a direct opportunity to answer. Honest ques-
tions rightly replace dishonest manipulation. What
results is an environment of trust in which you are free
to think and pray together about the question at hand,
as two people who want God’s will above their own.
Furthermore, questions – even bad ones – usually lead
to better questions, and to better conversation.
